opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting point for that project was a fairly simple question. Around 2021, Vision Transformers and especially Swin Transformers were beating ConvNets on ImageNet and on downstream tasks like detection and segmentation, and the common story was that self-attention itself was the key ingredient, that there was something fundamentally better about attention as an inductive bias, or the lack of one, compared to convolution.

But when we looked closely, we noticed that the transformer papers weren't only changing the core operator. They were also bringing along a whole package of other things: a different training recipe with much longer schedules, AdamW, heavy data augmentation like Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing. And a lot of macro and micro design choices, like the stage compute ratio, a patchify stem, fewer activation and normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, larger effective receptive fields, inverted bottlenecks. So it was really unclear how much of the gap came from attention and how much came from everything else.

So what we did was take a standard ResNet-50 and gradually "modernize" it, one step at a time, toward the design of a hierarchical vision transformer, while keeping it a pure ConvNet, and we measured accuracy at each step.

The first surprising thing was just the training recipe. Training the plain ResNet-50 with the modern transformer-style recipe already brought it from about 76.1 to around 78.8 percent top-1. That's a big chunk of the gap, with no architecture change at all. Many earlier comparisons were not apples to apples on this.

Then each design change gave a modest gain. Adjusting the stage ratio, using a patchify stem with a 4 by 4 non-overlapping convolution, going to depthwise convolutions and widening the network the way ResNeXt suggests, using an inverted bottleneck, moving to larger kernels like 7 by 7, which is kind of analogous to the local window size in Swin. Then the micro things: GELU instead of ReLU, far fewer activations and norms, LayerNorm, separate downsampling layers. None of these alone was dramatic, but together they added up, and the final ConvNeXt matched or slightly beat Swin at similar FLOPs, and scaled well too.

So the main lesson for me was that the apparent advantage of transformers in vision was not mainly about self-attention. A lot of it came from the training procedure and from a collection of design decisions that had accumulated over time, many of which are not specific to attention at all. Convolution as an operator was still perfectly competitive once you gave it the same treatment.

And I think the broader takeaway, which I care about, is methodological: when a new architecture wins, we should be careful about attributing the win to the headline component. You really need controlled ablations to know what's actually responsible. That doesn't mean transformers aren't great, they're very flexible and they unify modalities nicely, but for the specific question of "is attention what makes vision models good," the answer from that study was: much less than people thought.

r001.rationale: The response says each design change gave a modest gain and that none alone was dramatic.

r002.rationale: It says the gains added up across design choices and that the apparent transformer advantage was not mainly due to self-attention, but to training and design decisions that also apply to ConvNets.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that we learned the "transformer advantage" was mostly not about attention at all. When we started that project, the narrative in 2021 was that Swin Transformers had overtaken ResNets on vision tasks, and people were reading that as evidence that self-attention was fundamentally a better inductive bias than convolution. We were skeptical, because the comparison was never clean. A Swin Transformer and a ResNet-50 differ in dozens of ways beyond the core operator, and almost none of those had been isolated.

So we did something fairly boring on purpose. We took a standard ResNet-50 and, step by step, moved it toward the design of a Swin Transformer, keeping convolution the whole way, and measured ImageNet accuracy after each change. And the striking thing was how many small, unglamorous decisions each gave you a point or a fraction of a point, and how they added up.

The biggest buckets were roughly these. First, training recipe. Just training the plain ResNet-50 with the modern recipe, AdamW, longer schedules, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing, moved it from about 76 to about 78 percent. That alone accounted for a large part of the gap people were attributing to architecture. Second, macro design, meaning the stage compute ratio and a "patchify" stem with a 4 by 4 stride-4 convolution instead of the 7 by 7 conv plus max-pool. Third, going to depthwise convolutions with a wider network, which is really the ResNeXt idea, and that's where you see the parallel to attention: depthwise conv mixes information spatially per channel, and the pointwise convs mix across channels, which is structurally what the attention plus MLP blocks are doing too. Fourth, the inverted bottleneck and moving the depthwise conv earlier in the block. Fifth, larger kernels, 7 by 7, which gave you a bigger receptive field like the window size in Swin, and we found gains saturated there. And finally the micro details: GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activations and fewer normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, separate downsampling layers.

What I took away is that the field had been conflating "architecture" with "operator." The attention operator itself was not the thing. A lot of the gain came from the design choices that happened to travel along with transformers because the people building them came from NLP and brought those habits with them. Once a ConvNet adopted those same choices, it matched or beat Swin at similar compute, and it was simpler, with no shifted windows, no relative position biases, and it scaled on COCO and ADE20K too.

The other lesson, which I think is more about research methodology than about vision, is how much the baseline matters. A well-tuned old idea often beats a poorly tuned new idea, and the community tends to underinvest in tuning the old idea because it's not publishable. We tried to make the ablation path itself the contribution, so that people could see exactly where each point came from.

I would add one caveat, though. We did not conclude that convolution is better, or that attention has no role. Attention has real advantages in flexibility, especially for multimodal inputs and for scaling with data, and later work, including our own, mixed the two. The claim was narrower: the gap that existed at that time was not evidence of a superior operator. It was evidence of a superior recipe.

r001.rationale: The response says the many individual design decisions each added a point or a fraction of a point, and that their gains added up, communicating that no single ablation produced a large gain.

r002.rationale: It says the attention operator itself was not the source of the advantage and that adopting the accompanying design choices let a ConvNet match or beat Swin, emphasizing the combined design details over the core operation.

astra-6.text:
The main lesson was that the apparent transformer advantage wasn’t necessarily all coming from self-attention. There were many other differences bundled into that comparison: the training recipe, the architecture, and choices that had evolved over time.

We started with a standard ResNet and gradually modernized it, borrowing design choices from hierarchical vision transformers. As we changed the training setup, the stage structure, the block design, and things like kernel sizes and normalization, the gap narrowed. The resulting model, ConvNeXt, was still a pure convolutional network, but it could compete with transformers.

That doesn’t mean attention is unimportant. It means that comparing an older ConvNet with a carefully designed, modern transformer doesn’t isolate the value of attention. The ablations showed how much of the advantage could come from the surrounding design and training choices.

r001.rationale: The response describes gradually modernizing the model and narrowing the gap, but does not state that no individual ablation produced a large performance gain.

r002.rationale: The response says surrounding design and training choices contributed to the apparent advantage, but does not clearly state that their combined effect matters more than choosing convolution versus self-attention.

sol-6.1.text:
The main lesson was that the gap wasn’t simply convolution versus self-attention. When we modernized a ResNet using design choices and training practices associated with vision transformers, much of that gap disappeared.

We changed things like the stage structure, the patch-like stem, kernel sizes, and the organization of the blocks. The ablations helped us see which changes contributed, although their effects depended on the other choices already in the model. The resulting ConvNeXt could compete with hierarchical vision transformers using standard convolutions.

So I think the takeaway is that you have to be careful about attributing an entire performance improvement to attention. The training recipe and the surrounding architecture matter a lot. That doesn’t mean attention has no advantages, but it shows that convolution was a much stronger baseline than the comparisons at the time suggested.

r001.rationale: The response says ablation effects depended on other choices, but does not state that no single ablation produced a large performance gain.

r002.rationale: It says architecture and training practices matter and that the gap was not simply convolution versus attention, but does not clearly state that the combined effect of small architectural details matters more than the core operation.
